messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 63
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Oceania
  relationship_status: Widowed
  occupation: Construction Worker
  trauma_type: Physical abuse by romantic partner
  pcl5: 68

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Visual (Body Parts): Specific body parts associated with the event, Event Recall: Talking about the event, Event Involvement: People who are related to the event
  Maladaptive Strategies: Stay Near Exit: make sure to stay close to exit, Compulsive Spending: I spend money impulsively to distract or comfort myself, Avoid Conflict: Any situation that might involve disagreement or confrontation
  Threat: Startle to Sounds: I jump or startle at ordinary sounds that would not bother most people, Waking Alert: I wake during the night to check whether I am safe, Scanning Exits: I scan for exits as soon as I enter any room or building
  Negative Appraisals: Can't Rely on Self: I can't rely on myself, Weakness Belief: I am a weak person, Emotional Numbness: I feel dead inside

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Frank is a 63-year-old construction worker, a widower of nearly five years, who came to see me after his daughter insisted he talk to someone. He sat heavily in the chair, his large, calloused hands resting on his knees, and for a long moment he said nothing. When he finally spoke, it was about the woman who had been his partner for three years before she died. He did not call her his abuser. He said her name, then stopped. The story came out in fragments, as if he were still trying to assemble it himself.

The worst of it happened in the small house they shared. She was a volatile woman, quick to anger, and her violence was not the kind that left marks a man could explain away at work. She would strike him with whatever was near—a shoe, a lamp, her fists—but what he remembered most vividly was the way her hands looked when she was about to hit him. The tendons standing out, the knuckles white. He would see those hands coming and freeze. He told me once, his voice flat, that he had never hit her back. He had been raised not to hit a woman, and so he had stood there and taken it, night after night, until one night he simply stopped feeling anything at all.

Now, years later, those hands are everywhere. He cannot look at his own hands without a sick lurch in his stomach. He avoids looking at the hands of women he passes on the street. In the hardware store, he will cross an aisle to avoid a female cashier with large hands. At work, on the construction site, he is fine until a female project manager holds up a blueprint and points—and he sees her knuckles, and the world goes quiet, and he has to walk away. He tells himself he is being ridiculous. He knows she is not going to hit him. But knowing does not stop the cold wash of fear that comes over him.

He has become a man who lives by exits. When he walks onto a job site, the first thing he does is locate every door, every window, every possible way out. He sits with his back to the wall in the lunch trailer. He has left restaurants mid-meal because the only open seat was too far from the door. His daughter has stopped inviting him to family gatherings because he always leaves early, and she has begun to take it personally. He does not know how to explain that he is not rejecting her—he is simply certain, in a way that feels like fact, that he cannot trust himself to stay safe. He cannot rely on himself. That is what he says: "I can't rely on myself." He means it literally. He believes that if something dangerous happened, he would freeze again, just as he did with her. He sees his own inaction as proof of a fundamental weakness, a flaw in his character that makes him less than a man.

To manage the constant, low-grade dread, he has started spending money he does not have. He buys tools he does not need, electronics he never opens. The packages arrive, and for a few hours he feels something other than the hollow numbness that has settled inside him. He calls it "dead inside," and he means it. He does not feel joy. He does not feel anger, except in flashes that frighten him. He does not feel grief for his wife, who died of cancer two years after the relationship ended. He feels nothing, and then he feels guilty for feeling nothing, and then he spends more money.

Sleep is a problem. He wakes several times a night, heart pounding, convinced he needs to check that the doors are locked, that no one is in the house. He has no idea what he would do if someone were there—he cannot rely on himself, after all—but the compulsion is overwhelming. During the day, ordinary sounds make him jump: a car backfiring, a dropped hammer, a door slamming. His coworkers have started to notice. They joke that he is jumpy. He laughs along, but he is ashamed.

What finally brought him here was an incident at a diner. A woman at the next table raised her voice at a child, not even loudly, and Frank was out of his seat and out the door before he knew what he was doing. He stood in the parking lot, shaking, and realized he could not keep living this way. His daughter had been right. He needs help. He is afraid of what he might become if he does not get it—more isolated, more numb, more broke. But what he hopes, though he cannot say it aloud, is that someone will tell him he is not weak. That freezing was not a choice. That he can learn to trust himself again.
